title: Light at the End of the Tunnel: Warren's Shaft Theory of David's Conquest Shattered
author: Ronny Reich; Eli Shukron
allowedUseNotes: Copyrighted magazine article reporting peer excavation results. Project stores its own summary of the argument only; no reproduction of the article's text, plans, or photographs.
summary: Reich and Shukron's report of their own City of David excavations near the Gihon Spring, arguing against the long-standing popular reading of 2 Samuel 5:8's difficult word 'tsinnor' (rendered 'water shaft'/'watercourse' in most English translations) as a reference to the vertical karstic shaft known as Warren's Shaft (discovered 1867), by which David's men were traditionally imagined to have climbed into the Jebusite city. On the basis of their excavation of the surrounding Middle Bronze Age fortification and water-system complex, they argue Warren's Shaft itself was a natural karstic feature not deliberately incorporated into the water-drawing system until centuries after David's traditional date, and propose the shaft was not exposed/usable as an access route until roughly the 8th century BCE. This project cites Reich and Shukron as one named, checkable position within the wider unresolved debate over what 'tsinnor' refers to in 2 Samuel 5:8 (other proposed readings include a water channel/conduit generally, a grappling hook or weapon, or a term for a body part in a taunt) — not as having settled the question.
confidenceNotes: Full citation (BAR 25/1, Jan/Feb 1999, pp. 22-33, 72) and the argument summary are cross-corroborated across multiple independent secondary sources (Scientific Research Publishing's reference listing, Biblical Archaeology Society's own library index, and multiple third-party summaries of the Warren's Shaft dating debate, including Wikipedia's Warren's Shaft article), not from direct inspection of the article itself. TO VERIFY: exact page-level detail of the excavation evidence cited for the later-exposure argument, against a physical or full-digital copy. This project does not resolve which reading of 'tsinnor' (water shaft, general conduit, weapon, or body-part idiom) is correct; the underlying Hebrew is widely described in the secondary literature as one of the most difficult textual cruxes in Samuel.
